answer:
Only the analyzer reads `analysis_options.yaml`: it decides which diagnostics are produced and at what severity, and the compiler never opens the file — so a genuine type error fails the build whatever you write there.

### The three severities
- **error**, **warning**, **info** is the whole list. A lint rule reports at info unless you say otherwise.
- **error** — something the compiler will also reject, or a diagnostic you promoted yourself.
- **warning** — legal code the analyzer believes is wrong: `unused_import`, `dead_code`.
- **info** — every lint rule, plus advisory diagnostics.
- There used to be a fourth bucket called **hint**; it was retired, and `unused_import` and `dead_code` moved to warning. The word still shows up in old posts and in `flutter analyze --help`.

### What the file actually controls
- `include:` — the published ruleset you inherit.
- `linter: rules:` — which lint rules run.
- `analyzer: errors:` — the severity of any diagnostic code, `ignore` included.
- `analyzer: exclude:` — paths the analyzer never looks at.
- `analyzer: language:` — `strict-casts`, `strict-inference`, `strict-raw-types`.
- `formatter: page_width:` — since Dart 3.7, so the IDE and `dart format` agree on width.

### Which severity actually fails CI
- `dart analyze` treats warnings as fatal and infos as not; `--fatal-infos` adds them.
- `flutter analyze` treats infos as fatal by default as well. Same rules, same code, two exit codes — so pass the flag you mean instead of inheriting a default.

The mental model: the diagnostic is the fact, the severity is your policy, and the compiler is not part of the negotiation.
code_example:
# analysis_options.yaml — everything the analyzer reads about this package
include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml    # inherit a published ruleset

analyzer:
  exclude:                        # not analysed at all: no lints, no errors
    - "**/*.g.dart"
    - "**/*.freezed.dart"
  errors:                         # severity of ANY diagnostic code
    use_build_context_synchronously: error   # info -> breaks the build
    invalid_annotation_target: ignore        # freezed + json_serializable noise
    dead_code: error                         # already a warning; promoted
  language:
    strict-casts: true

linter:
  rules:
    unawaited_futures: true       # not in flutter_lints; opt in by hand
    prefer_single_quotes: false   # map form is the only way to switch one OFF

formatter:
  page_width: 100                 # Dart 3.7+; replaces passing --line-length

# $ dart analyze
#   error   - lib/a.dart:2:3 - ...                          - dead_code
#   warning - lib/a.dart:1:8 - Unused import: 'dart:math'.   - unused_import
#   info    - lib/a.dart:9:3 - Don't invoke 'print' ...      - avoid_print
#
# dart analyze                 -> exit 1 on the error and the warning only
# dart analyze --fatal-infos   -> exit 1 on all three
# flutter analyze              -> exit 1 on all three already (fatal-infos is on)

answer:
You go from roughly a hundred rules to a hundred and ninety-three, `dart fix` clears most of the new findings mechanically, and what it cannot fix is the style argument you are really having.

### What the three sets are
- `package:lints` is the Dart team's baseline. `core.yaml` is 35 rules for things that are almost always bugs; `recommended.yaml` includes core and adds idiomatic-style rules on top. No Flutter knowledge at all.
- `package:flutter_lints` includes `lints/recommended` and adds exactly ten Flutter rules — `avoid_print`, `use_build_context_synchronously`, `use_key_in_widget_constructors`, `sized_box_for_whitespace`, `no_logic_in_create_state` among them. This is what `flutter create` writes for you.
- `package:very_good_analysis` is 193 rules. It adds `public_member_api_docs`, `lines_longer_than_80_chars`, `require_trailing_commas`, `avoid_dynamic_calls`, `unawaited_futures` and the whole `prefer_const_*` family that flutter_lints leaves off.

### The morning after
- Run `dart fix --dry-run` first. It prints a count per diagnostic, and that count is the mechanical share.
- What survives is doc comments and line lengths: hundreds of findings, no automated fix, no bug behind any of them.
- Switch a rule off with the map form, `rule_name: false`. The list form can only enable, so you cannot drop an inherited rule with it.
- These are packages. `dart pub upgrade` can add rules and redden CI with no code change, so pin the version and bump it on purpose.
- A rule the SDK has since removed turns into an `undefined_lint` warning pointing at your own options file.

Adopt the strictest set the team will actually fix, not the strictest set that exists — a ruleset nobody obeys just teaches people to write `// ignore_for_file`.
code_example:
# --- What flutter create gives you: lints/core + lints/recommended + 10 rules
include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml

# --- The strict end: 193 rules, docs and line length included
# include: package:very_good_analysis/analysis_options.yaml

# --- Pure Dart package, no Flutter: 35 rules that are almost always bugs
# include: package:lints/core.yaml

linter:
  rules:
    # LIST form can only switch rules ON — it cannot drop an inherited one.
    - unawaited_futures

    # MAP form is the only way to disable something the include brought in.
    # public_member_api_docs: false
    # lines_longer_than_80_chars: false
    # require_trailing_commas: false

# pubspec.yaml — the ruleset is a package, so its version is a policy decision
# dev_dependencies:
#   flutter_lints: 6.0.0            # exact, not ^6.0.0: a minor bump adds
#                                   # rules and reddens CI with no code change
#
# $ dart fix --dry-run              # how much of the new set is mechanical
# $ dart fix --apply                # land the ruleset and the fixes together
#
# Delete a rule the SDK dropped, or the analyzer flags your own file:
#   warning - analysis_options.yaml:5:5 - '...' is not a recognized lint rule.

answer:
Promote the rules whose violations are bugs a reviewer cannot see — the async and context ones — and leave naming, layout and documentation at info, because a style rule that breaks the build gets an ignore comment rather than a fix.

### What the block does
- `analyzer: errors:` maps any diagnostic code — a lint or an analyzer diagnostic — onto `error`, `warning`, `info` or `ignore`.
- It changes the severity and therefore the exit code. The message and the rule behind it are untouched.
- It works downwards too, which is how `invalid_annotation_target` from freezed gets silenced in one place instead of a comment in every model file.

### Worth promoting
- `use_build_context_synchronously` — a crash after an await, invisible in a diff.
- `unawaited_futures` — an exception with nowhere to go.
- `unrelated_type_equality_checks` and `collection_methods_unrelated_type` — comparisons that compile and are always false.
- `hash_and_equals` — a `Set` that quietly stops de-duplicating.
- `deprecated_member_use`, but only once the last call site is gone; before that it is noise people learn to scroll past.

### Not worth promoting
- `public_member_api_docs`, `lines_longer_than_80_chars`, `sort_constructors_first`, `always_specify_types` — real preferences with no runtime consequence, and the fastest way to normalise ignore comments.
- The mirror mistake is demoting to keep CI green: `deprecated_member_use: ignore` deletes the only reminder you had that a migration is pending.

The test to apply per rule: would you revert a release for it? If yes, `error`. If it would only have made the diff prettier, leave it at info and let review carry it.
code_example:
include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml

analyzer:
  errors:
    # --- Promoted: each one is a bug class review cannot see ---
    use_build_context_synchronously: error   # crash after an await
    unawaited_futures: error                 # exception with nowhere to go
    unrelated_type_equality_checks: error    # 'a' == 1 compiles, always false
    collection_methods_unrelated_type: error # list.remove(wrongType) removes 0
    hash_and_equals: error                   # Set silently stops de-duplicating

    # --- Demoted on purpose, with the reason in the file ---
    invalid_annotation_target: ignore        # freezed/json_serializable, known
    todo: ignore                             # TODOs are not a release blocker

    # --- What NOT to do ---
    # public_member_api_docs: error     # style; becomes // ignore_for_file
    # lines_longer_than_80_chars: error # the formatter's job, not the gate's
    # deprecated_member_use: ignore     # deletes the reminder to migrate

linter:
  rules:
    unawaited_futures: true    # promoting a rule you never enabled does nothing

# Severity changes the exit code, not the text:
#   info  - lib/a.dart:4:5 - ... - use_build_context_synchronously
#   error - lib/a.dart:4:5 - ... - use_build_context_synchronously

Ask for a line-level `// ignore:` with a comment saying why, because the file-level form also silences code nobody has written yet, and `exclude` removes the file from analysis entirely — errors included.

### The three hatches, narrowest first
- `// ignore: rule_a, rule_b` on its own line covers the next line; at the end of a line it covers that line. It is the only form scoped tightly enough that a reviewer can see what is being hidden.
- `// ignore_for_file: rule` covers the whole file, including everything added to it later. `// ignore_for_file: type=lint` silences every lint in the file in one line.
- `analyzer: exclude:` takes the path out of analysis: no lints, no warnings, no errors, forever. Correct for generated output, wrong for a directory you intend to clean up.

### Two things reviewers miss
- An `// ignore:` on a real compile error silences `dart analyze` and the build still fails — the compiler does not read comments, so a green analyze step can sit in front of a broken build.
- Ignores never expire. Neither flutter_lints nor very_good_analysis enables `unnecessary_ignore`, the rule that reports an ignore for a diagnostic no longer produced there; turn it on and a batch of dead ones surfaces immediately.

### Making a rule un-ignorable
- `analyzer: cannot-ignore:` lists diagnostic codes that no comment can suppress. That is the home for the two or three rules you genuinely mean, and it is the answer when the same `// ignore:` keeps reappearing in review.

The hatch should be as small as the problem. An ignore with no reason beside it is a TODO nobody will ever find.

Both sides run the same `package:analyzer`, so the difference is never the tool — it is the inputs: the SDK, the resolved dependency versions, what is actually on disk, and which folders are in scope.

### The four inputs, in the order they bite
1. **SDK version.** The IDE analyses with whatever Dart it is pointed at — an fvm symlink, a system install, a bundled one — while CI usually takes whichever `stable` shipped that week. A new SDK adds diagnostics and moves existing ones between severities, and neither of you changed a line.
2. **Resolved dependencies.** A `pub get` that ignores the lockfile resolves newer packages on the runner, and a member deprecated in that newer version is flagged only there. `dart pub get --enforce-lockfile` fails instead of silently upgrading.
3. **Files on disk.** The `.g.dart` and `.freezed.dart` from a build you ran last week exist in your tree and not in a fresh clone; a file you forgot to `git add` analyses perfectly on your machine and does not exist in CI.
4. **Scope.** `flutter analyze` covers the current package only, `dart analyze <dir>` walks a directory, and the IDE analyses the folders you opened minus whatever its own settings exclude. In a monorepo those three sets are rarely the same set.

### Reproducing it in ten seconds
- Clone your own branch into a temp directory and run the exact CI commands there. The difference announces itself.
- If the IDE looks stale after you edit `analysis_options.yaml` or `pubspec.yaml`, restart the analysis server before believing it.

Treat the editor as a fast preview of one configuration and CI as the definition of it; when they disagree, make the inputs equal rather than argue with the output.
code_example:
# Editor green, CI red. Make the inputs identical, in this order.

# 1. Same SDK the job uses — the IDE must point at the same one
fvm use 3.35.0 && fvm flutter --version
dart --version

# 2. Same package versions: without this CI is free to resolve newer ones
dart pub get --enforce-lockfile      # fails instead of silently upgrading

# 3. Same files: analyse a clean clone, not your working tree.
#    .g.dart from last week's build exists here and nowhere else.
git clone --branch "$(git branch --show-current)" . /tmp/verify
cd /tmp/verify && dart pub get --enforce-lockfile
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

# 4. Same scope and the same fatality, spelled out rather than inherited
dart analyze --fatal-infos .         # dart:    infos are NOT fatal by default
flutter analyze                      # flutter: infos ARE fatal by default
                                     # and it covers this package only

# Still disagreeing? Print what each side is actually reading.
dart --version
cat analysis_options.yaml
dart pub deps --style=compact | head -20

Dart 3.7 replaced the formatter's style, and the new one is chosen by the package's language version rather than by a flag — so raising your SDK constraint reformats the repository, which is exactly why it has to be a commit of its own listed in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`.

### What the tall style changed
- A trailing comma is no longer a force-split marker. The formatter decides where to split and adds or removes trailing commas itself, so the old trick of leaving a trailing comma to keep one argument per line is gone.
- Long expressions and arrow bodies indent differently, which is why the diff reaches files nobody edited.
- Page width moved into `analysis_options.yaml` as `formatter: page_width:`, so the IDE, `dart format` and CI finally agree without anyone passing `--line-length`.

### dart fix, in the same cleanup
- `dart fix --dry-run` prints a count per diagnostic; `--apply` writes them; `--code=prefer_const_constructors` narrows it to one rule so the PR stays reviewable.
- It only fixes diagnostics that have a fix producer behind them — a lint with none is manual work no matter how mechanical it looks.
- Packages can ship a `fix_data.yaml`, so `dart fix` also rewrites callers across a package's own deprecations. That is how a rename in a shared package migrates its consumers.

### The blame cost, and the cure
- Reformat in a commit containing no logic, append that SHA to `.git-blame-ignore-revs`, and set `blame.ignoreRevsFile`. GitHub reads the file with no configuration at all.
- Land it when few branches are open, and tell people to rebase and re-run the formatter instead of resolving whitespace conflicts by hand.

Any commit whose diff is entirely whitespace goes in alone, and goes in the ignore file.
code_example:
# What actually changed: the tall style ships in Dart 3.7 and is selected by
# the package's language version, so bumping `environment: sdk:` reformats
# the repo. No flag turns it off.
cat > lib/f.dart <<'DART'
int add(int a, int b,) => a + b;
void main() {
  final x = add(
    1,
    2,
  );
  print(x);
}
DART

dart format --output=show lib/f.dart
#   int add(int a, int b) => a + b;        <- trailing comma removed
#   final x = add(1, 2);                   <- no longer forces one arg per line

# Land the mechanical lint debt first, one rule at a time so it stays reviewable
dart fix --dry-run
dart fix --apply --code=prefer_const_constructors
git commit -am "chore: dart fix --code=prefer_const_constructors"

# Then the reformat, alone, with nothing else in it
dart format .
git commit -am "chore: reformat with the Dart 3.7 tall style"

# Teach blame to skip it; GitHub honours this file with no extra config
git rev-parse HEAD >> .git-blame-ignore-revs
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
git commit -am "chore: ignore the reformat commit in blame"

# CI keeps it that way
dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .

A minority do, and they are worth naming: the const family decides whether whole subtrees rebuild, and a small correctness group catches comparisons and overrides that are silently wrong at runtime.

### const, and what it actually buys
- `Element.updateChild` reuses the existing child element untouched when the new widget is `==` to the old one, and Dart canonicalises const values — so the same const expression yields the identical object on every build and the subtree is skipped rather than rebuilt.
- The trap: **flutter_lints does not enable `prefer_const_constructors`.** It only enables `prefer_const_constructors_in_immutables`. Most teams assume the whole family is on. `very_good_analysis` has it; otherwise you add it yourself.
- The win exists only where the parent rebuilds often, so const in a `build` that runs once buys nothing measurable.

### The correctness handful
- `unrelated_type_equality_checks` — `'7' == 7` compiles and is always false.
- `collection_methods_unrelated_type` — `ids.remove(stringId)` removes nothing, silently. This rule replaced `iterable_contains_unrelated_type` and `list_remove_unrelated_type`.
- `hash_and_equals` — an `==` with no matching `hashCode`, and your `Set` stops de-duplicating.
- `no_logic_in_create_state` — `createState` can run more than once for the same widget, so anything computed there from constructor arguments goes stale.

### The cheap ones that still cost frames
- `avoid_unnecessary_containers` and `sized_box_for_whitespace` each remove a `RenderObject` from every build of that subtree.

Split the ruleset into rules that change the app and rules that change the diff. The first group earns `error`; the second is a review preference, and the formatter already settles most of it.

A token in the device log, an exception nobody ever sees, and a crash on a screen the user has already left.

### avoid_print
- `print` is not stripped from release builds. It writes to logcat and the iOS device console, so whatever you interpolated — a bearer token, an email, a response body — ships with the app and turns up in bug reports and crash attachments.
- Android also drops log lines when they arrive too fast, which is why `debugPrint` throttles. A print-based log is not even a reliable log.
- It is on in flutter_lints already. Replace it with a logger that has levels, or at minimum `dart:developer`'s `log` behind `kDebugMode`.

### unawaited_futures
- A dropped `await` in an async body leaves the error with nowhere to go: it surfaces as an unhandled async error whose stack points at the framework, or it is swallowed by whatever zone caught it.
- The other half is ordering — you pop the route before the write commits, and the previous screen reads stale data.
- It is **not** in flutter_lints or lints; you enable it. Mark deliberate fire-and-forget calls with `unawaited()` from `dart:async`, which is exactly what the rule looks for. `discarded_futures` is the stricter neighbour for synchronous code.

### use_build_context_synchronously
- After an await the element can be defunct, and `Navigator.of(context)` then throws "Looking up a deactivated widget's ancestor is unsafe" — the crash users hit by backgrounding the app mid-request.
- Put `if (!context.mounted) return;` between the gap and the use; the lint understands that guard and goes quiet.
- Capture `ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)` before the await when a snackbar is all you need. It is on in flutter_lints.

All three share a shape: each replaces a bug class you cannot see in a diff. That is the test for whether a rule earns a place in the ruleset.

Write it as a `custom_lint` rule: a small Dart package the analysis server loads, which is handed the resolved AST of each file and whose diagnostics show up in the IDE and in CI.

### What the rule can see
- Add `custom_lint` as a dev dependency, `custom_lint_builder` in the package that holds the rules, and list `custom_lint` under `analyzer: plugins:` in `analysis_options.yaml`.
- A rule extends `DartLintRule`, declares a `LintCode`, and subscribes to node types through `context.registry.addInstanceCreationExpression`, `addMethodInvocation` and friends.
- Types are resolved, so you can ask which package a symbol came from rather than how it is spelled — that is the whole difference between a rule and a grep.
- A rule can ship its own correction: a `DartFix` attached to it becomes an IDE quick fix and a `dart fix --apply` edit. `riverpod_lint` and `bloc_lint` are exactly this, published.

### What it cannot see
- One library at a time. "Nobody calls this any more" and "this file is orphaned" are whole-program questions the plugin API does not answer cheaply.
- Nothing at runtime, and nothing in files that have not been generated yet — a rule about `*.g.dart` output only sees it after `build_runner` has run.

### What it costs
- `dart analyze` does not run custom_lint rules. CI needs `dart run custom_lint` as its own step, or the rule only exists for whoever has the IDE open.
- The plugin runs in a separate process per analysis context, warms up for a few seconds, and re-runs your rule on every keystroke. Bail out early on files that cannot match, and use registry callbacks instead of walking the tree yourself.

Write the rule once the same comment has been made three times and has a mechanical test. Anything fuzzier than that stays a conversation.

The analyzer only reports what it can prove inside one library — private declarations and unreachable statements — so everything public, every dependency and every asset needs a separate whole-repo pass.

### What the analyzer already catches
- `unused_import`, `unused_local_variable`, `unused_field`, `unused_element` and `dead_code`.
- The unused-declaration diagnostics fire for private names only. A public class nobody imports is invisible to them, because some other package might import it tomorrow — the analyzer cannot know it is not a library.
- Promoting those from info to warning in `analysis_options.yaml` is free and catches the daily kind.

### What needs a tool
- Unused public code and whole unreferenced files: DCM's `dcm check-unused-code` and `dcm check-unused-files`. The open-source `dart_code_metrics` was retired into DCM, so this one costs money now.
- Unused packages: `dependency_validator` reports dependencies nothing imports, and imports with no declared dependency. The second half is the one that breaks someone else's build later.
- What actually shipped: `flutter build apk --analyze-size` (also `appbundle`, `ipa`) prints the tree of everything that landed in the artefact, and DevTools opens the JSON. That is ground truth for assets and for a package you assumed was tree-shaken.

### What nothing can know
- Anything reached through a string: `Image.asset('icons/$name.png')`, a route table built from a map, a `@pragma('vm:entry-point')` callback the platform calls, code only the tests use.
- So treat every "unused" report as a question, not a verdict. Delete on the evidence of a size analysis plus a repo-wide search, and do it in its own commit so reverting is one click.
code_example:
# 1. What the analyzer already knows — private declarations, unreachable code.
dart analyze --fatal-infos

# 2. Dependencies nothing imports, and imports with no dependency.
dart pub global activate dependency_validator
dart run dependency_validator

# 3. Public code and whole files nothing references (DCM, commercial).
dcm check-unused-code lib
dcm check-unused-files lib

# 4. Assets: no first-party tool exists, but a grep is honest enough.
find assets -type f | while read -r f; do
  name=$(basename "$f")
  if ! grep -Rq --include='*.dart' -F "$name" lib && ! grep -q -F "$f" pubspec.yaml; then
    echo "orphan candidate: $f"
  fi
done

# 5. Ground truth: what actually landed in the artefact.
flutter build apk --release --analyze-size --target-platform android-arm64
#   prints every asset and package in the APK, and writes a JSON DevTools opens

# The trap all five steps share is the string:
#   Image.asset('icons/$name.png')   -> grep sees "icons/", never the filename
#   @pragma('vm:entry-point')        -> no Dart caller exists at all
#   routes['/checkout']              -> the class is only named in a map
# Delete in a commit of its own, so the revert is one click.

Take it as a signal on the diff, never as a gate on the repository — the number tells you which file is worth reading and nothing at all about whether the code is good.

### Where they sharpen a review
- Nesting depth and parameter count track real trouble closely enough to be worth an alert; they are hard to hit by accident and hard to fake away.
- A metric that moved in this pull request is a useful "look here", even when the absolute value is still fine.
- Capping new files while leaving existing ones alone gets most of the benefit with none of the migration.

### Where they turn into theatre
- Cyclomatic complexity is a bad fit for Flutter. A 400-line `build` with one `if` scores 2 and is genuinely hard to read; a `switch` over a sealed state with ten arms scores 11 and is the clearest code in the file.
- The gate is trivial to game: split `build` into `_buildHeader`, `_buildBody`, `_buildFooter` and every threshold passes, while the code got worse — those private builders cannot be `const` and rebuild with the whole widget.
- Any number you fail the build on becomes a target and stops measuring what you cared about.

### How to configure them so they survive
- Exclude generated code (`*.g.dart`, `*.freezed.dart`, `*.gr.dart`) and `test/`. A 2000-line generated file teaches nobody anything and trains people to ignore the report.
- Set each threshold where it flags roughly the worst five percent of today's code, and surface them as warnings on the pull request rather than as a red build.

Metrics choose what gets read; people decide what gets changed.
code_example:
# analysis_options.yaml
include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml

analyzer:
  exclude:
    - "**/*.g.dart"
    - "**/*.freezed.dart"
    - build/**

# DCM metrics. Reported on the pull request, not wired to the exit code.
dart_code_metrics:
  metrics:
    cyclomatic-complexity: 20      # deliberately loose: build() skews it badly
    maximum-nesting-level: 4       # the one that actually tracks pain
    number-of-parameters: 5
    source-lines-of-code: 60
  metrics-exclude:
    - test/**
    - "**/*.g.dart"
    - lib/l10n/**
  rules:
    - avoid-passing-async-when-sync-expected
    - avoid-unnecessary-setstate

# What the config above does and does not buy you:
#
#   Widget build(BuildContext context) {       // 400 lines, complexity 2
#     return Column(children: [ /* ... */ ]);  // metric: fine.  review: not fine.
#   }
#
#   switch (state) {                           // 10 sealed arms, complexity 11
#     case Loading():  ...                     // metric: flagged.
#     case Failure():  ...                     // review: clearest code in the file.
#   }
#
# And the move that passes every threshold above while making the widget
# rebuild more: chop build() into _buildHeader / _buildBody / _buildFooter.

Add the new name, mark the old one `@Deprecated` with a message that names the replacement, keep both through at least one release, and delete it only in a major version.

### What the analyzer does for callers
- `@Deprecated('Use parseUser instead. Removed in 3.0.0.')` — the message is required; the bare `@deprecated` shorthand carries none and `provide_deprecation_message` flags it.
- Callers in another package get `deprecated_member_use`. Callers inside your own package get the separate `deprecated_member_use_from_same_package`, so you can silence your own migration noise without hiding anything from consumers.
- Both are warnings. `dart analyze` treats warnings as fatal by default, so a consumer's CI turns red while `flutter run` still builds — which is exactly the right amount of pressure.
- Keep one implementation: the deprecated member forwards to the new one. Two bodies drift, and then the deprecation ships a bug.

### The removal window
- SemVer: deprecate in a minor, remove in a major, never both in the same release. Flutter's own framework policy holds a deprecation for at least a year and several stable releases.
- Announce it where consumers actually read — the changelog entry, not only the annotation.

### Migrating callers for free
- Ship `lib/fix_data.yaml` with the package. `dart fix --apply` in the consumer's repo then rewrites their call sites for them, and their IDE offers it as a quick fix.
- The transforms cover renames, added, removed and renamed parameters, and moving a member to another class.

A deprecation nobody announces and nobody automates is a breaking change with extra steps.

All four are enforced, but only by the analyzer and only as warnings — nothing stops the code compiling, running or shipping.

### What each one checks
- `@visibleForTesting`: use outside the declaring library and outside the package's `test` directory is `invalid_use_of_visible_for_testing_member`.
- `@protected`: access is allowed inside the declaring library and inside instance members of subclasses; anywhere else is `invalid_use_of_protected_member`.
- `@immutable`: the class, or any subclass of it, declaring a non-final field is `must_be_immutable`.
- `@mustCallSuper`: an override that never invokes `super.method()` is `must_call_super`.

### What each one does not check
- `@visibleForTesting` removes nothing from the release build. The member is still compiled, still exported, still callable — the annotation is a note, not an access modifier.
- `@immutable` is shallow. `final List<String> tags` passes, and so does a final field holding a `ChangeNotifier`. It says nothing about `==`, `hashCode` or `const`.
- `@mustCallSuper` only checks that the call appears somewhere in the body — not where, not on which branch, not whether you already tore down the thing `super` needs. `if (kDebugMode) super.dispose();` satisfies it.
- `@protected` is not Java's `protected`. It sits on an ordinary public member; any code can still call it, and a `dynamic` receiver walks straight past.

### The part that is only documentation
- The severity. All four land as warnings in `dart analyze` and are invisible to `flutter build`, so on a team that reads warnings as decoration they buy nothing at all.
- Promote the ones you mean under `analyzer: errors:` in `analysis_options.yaml`, and treat the rest as what they are: notes to the next reader.

CI is the gate and the hook is only a convenience, because hooks live in `.git/hooks`, which is never cloned, and `git commit --no-verify` skips them by design.

### What belongs in the hook
- Fast, staged files only, and self-fixing: `dart format` on the staged Dart files, `dart fix --apply` on the same list, at most `dart analyze` on the touched directories.
- Budget about two seconds. Past that people reach for `--no-verify`, and they are right to.
- Anything the hook rewrites has to be re-staged, or the commit carries the version from before the fix — that is what lefthook's `stage_fixed: true` exists for, and it is the single most common reason "the hook runs but commits still arrive unformatted".

### What belongs in CI
- The whole repository, no auto-fixing, a non-zero exit: `dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .`, `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, `dart run custom_lint` (which `dart analyze` does not run), then the tests.
- CI is the only place with a guarantee. It runs on the merge result, from a clean checkout, with the SDK pinned by the workflow instead of by whatever each laptop happens to have.

### Making the hook actually install
- Never hand-edit `.git/hooks`. Either commit a `.githooks/` directory and set `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, or use a manager — lefthook, husky, `pre-commit` — and call its install from the same bootstrap script new joiners already run.
- Have the hook print what it is doing and how to skip it. A silent hook that eats twenty seconds is uninstalled within a week.

If a check can only pass locally, it is not a check. The hook saves you a round trip; CI decides.
code_example:
# lefthook.yml — committed. `lefthook install` wires .git/hooks on every clone.
pre-commit:
  parallel: true
  commands:
    format:
      glob: "*.dart"
      run: dart format {staged_files}
      stage_fixed: true      # without this the commit keeps the pre-format bytes
    fix:
      glob: "*.dart"
      run: dart fix --apply {staged_files}
      stage_fixed: true
    analyze:
      glob: "*.dart"
      run: dart analyze {staged_files}
# Nothing slower belongs here. No full test suite, no `flutter build`.
# Skipping is a supported move, not a crime:  git commit --no-verify

---
# .github/workflows/analyze.yml — the gate. Nothing here can be --no-verify'd.
name: analyze
on: pull_request
jobs:
  static:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml   # the repo pins it, not the runner
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .
      - run: dart analyze --fatal-infos
      - run: dart run custom_lint     # dart analyze does NOT run these rules
      - run: flutter test

answer:
Turn the whole ruleset on and demote every rule it lights up to `ignore` in the same commit, then delete entries from that ignore list one pull request at a time.

### The one-commit switch
- Dart has no baseline file the way detekt or ESLint do, so the `analyzer: errors:` block in `analysis_options.yaml` is your baseline: a committed, reviewable list that visibly shrinks, with the issue count and a ticket beside each line.
- Run `dart fix --apply` first. It clears the mechanical half — often most of the count — and that commit reviews as "machine-generated, no manual edits". `dart fix --apply --code=<rule>` does one rule at a time when the whole thing is still too big to read.
- Then rank what is left. `dart analyze --format=machine` prints pipe-separated fields, so cutting out the rule column and counting gives you issues per rule in one line of shell.

### Burning the list down
- Take the rules with real bugs behind them first, regardless of count — `use_build_context_synchronously`, `unawaited_futures`, `cancel_subscriptions` — then the cheapest per issue.
- When the mess is geographic rather than per-rule, drop a second `analysis_options.yaml` inside the legacy directory; the analyzer uses the nearest one walking up. Prefer that to `exclude:`, which also hides genuine errors in those paths and is quietly forgotten within a quarter.

### Keeping it from growing back
- Analyze only the files the pull request changed, so new code meets the full bar while the backlog waits. Or ratchet: store the issue count, fail when it rises.
- Add the mass-fix commit to `.git-blame-ignore-revs`, or you have traded 4 000 warnings for a blame view that points at you on every line.
code_example:
# 1. The machine-fixable half, in its own commit, with zero manual edits.
dart fix --dry-run                     # what would change, and under which rule
dart fix --apply                       # or: --code=prefer_const_constructors
git commit -am "chore: dart fix --apply (machine-generated, no manual edits)"
git rev-parse HEAD >> .git-blame-ignore-revs
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

# 2. Rank what is left. --format=machine is pipe-separated; field 3 is the rule.
dart analyze --format=machine . | cut -d'|' -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
#   1841 prefer_const_constructors
#    612 always_declare_return_types
#     37 use_build_context_synchronously   <- take this one first anyway

# 3. Baseline: the ruleset goes on, today's noise is demoted in the same commit.
cat >> analysis_options.yaml <<'YAML'
analyzer:
  errors:
    prefer_const_constructors: ignore     # 1841 — burning down, see #4821
    always_declare_return_types: ignore   #  612 — see #4822
YAML

# 4. Stop the backlog growing: the full bar, on the diff only.
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=d origin/main... -- '*.dart' \
  | xargs -r dart analyze --fatal-infos

answer:
Everything that depends on conditions the diff does not show — lifecycle, states the code can reach but the tests never do, the failure path, and whether the change belongs in the layer it landed in.

### What no linter can see
- Ownership: is every controller, subscription and notifier created here also disposed here, and does the widget survive being rebuilt with new constructor arguments (`didUpdateWidget`)?
- State shape: can this class represent "loading and error at the same time"? No lint can ask whether the impossible state is unrepresentable.
- The unhappy paths: no network, permission denied, an empty list, 300% text scale, rotation mid-request. Most of these you find by running the branch, not by reading it.
- Boundaries: a `Response` or a `Dio` leaking into the widget layer, a repository constructed inside `build`, a user-visible string that never reached the l10n file.
- Tests that assert the implementation — a mock was called — instead of the behaviour a user gets.

### How to raise it
- Label the severity so the author can triage: `blocking:`, `suggestion:`, `nit:`, and say once, in the team doc, that anything unlabelled is a nit.
- Ask the question you actually have — "what happens if this fires twice?" — instead of prescribing a rewrite. Give the reason; the author usually knows a better fix than yours.
- Approve with comments for everything non-blocking. A second round trip costs the author a day of paged-in context and buys a comma.

### The review that costs the least
- Small pull requests, a description that says where to look, a screen recording for UI work.
- Any comment you have now made three times becomes a lint, a template or a CODEOWNERS rule — that is the whole point of owning your own analysis config.

The linter owns consistency; the reviewer owns consequences.
